conventions.convention: Tensor products are algebraic over a field; R is a finite tensor sum. Triple tensors are left-associated, with canonical reassociation inserted explicitly.
The quasitriangular equations are RΔ(h)=Δop(h)R, (Δ⊗id)R=R13R23, and α⁻¹(id⊗Δ)R=R13R12.
Braiding means a natural family of H-linear isomorphisms on all left H-modules satisfying both hexagons. Triangular means R21R=1⊗1; symmetric means c(W,V)c(V,W)=id.
The associated braiding is c(V,W)=τ(ρV⊗ρW)(R), so R=Σ ai⊗bi sends v⊗w to Σ biw⊗aiv. Reconstruction includes the regular module and imposes no finite-dimensionality assumption.
Local operators are indexed by 1≤i<n for n≥2; adjacent relations require i<n−1. No Hecke quadratic relation follows from quasitriangularity alone.
The scalar counterexample is over Q with R=2(1⊗1), so its first-hexagon coefficients 2 and 4 differ.

load_bearing.statement: An algebraic quasitriangular structure is an invertible R∈H⊗H satisfying RΔ(h)=Δop(h)R for every h, (Δ⊗id)R=R13R23, and α⁻¹(id⊗Δ)R=R13R12.

For a Hopf algebra over a field, an algebraic quasitriangular R gives a braiding on all left modules by c=τ(ρ⊗ρ)(R). The associated operator satisfies the braid relation, and symmetry is equivalent to R21R=1⊗1. Conversely, every braiding on all left modules uniquely determines an algebraic quasitriangular R=τc(H,H)(1⊗1), without finite-dimensionality assumptions.
For an invertible quasitriangular R in a Hopf algebra over a field, (ε⊗id)R=1=(id⊗ε)R and R12R13R23=R23R13R12.

For a unital algebra A over a field and n=2,3, equality of left-multiplication maps on the componentwise algebra A⊗n implies equality of their defining tensors; evaluation at 1⊗n recovers the defining tensor.

A braiding on all left H-modules is a natural family of H-linear isomorphisms satisfying both canonical-associator hexagons. A quasitriangular R is triangular if R21R=1⊗1, and a braiding is symmetric if c(W,V)c(V,W)=id for every V,W.

published_dependencies.used_for: Field scalars, finite algebraic tensor sums, left-associated tensor powers, and componentwise leg calculations.
Canonical reassociation, naturality and coherence in the leg definitions, module hexagons, and extension of local braid relations to tensor powers.
Componentwise tensor-algebra multiplication and its unit, including the regular tensor-algebra detection lemma.
Regular-module unit evaluation in the all-module reconstruction theorem; its first-factor regular action is distinguished from componentwise tensor-algebra multiplication.

concerns.concern: The Example concludes, “Then $D(k^G)$ is a four-dimensional Hopf algebra and $R$ is its canonical quasitriangular structure.” Its functions-first basis p_x#u_g and tensor R=Σ(p_x#u_e)⊗q_x instead instantiate D(kG) under def-hh-finite-double-cross-relations and thm-hh-finite-double-hopf-structure-and-canonical-r. This is also exactly the specialization of ex-drinfeld-double-of-a-finite-group. For H=k^G, the general canonical tensor has the group-dual factor first; transporting through the natural factor flip gives the example's R21, not R. These tensors differ: the coefficient of (p_e#u_s)⊗(p_s#u_e) is 0 in R and 1 in R21. No alternative identification transporting the canonical structure is supplied. The local Hopf and quasitriangular calculations are sound, but the claimed canonical identification with D(k^G) needs adjudication.

seams_checked.note: The Hopf interface supplies unital algebra-map coproduct and counit, coalgebra identities, and a convolution antipode. Batch 8 adds no assumption that the antipode is compositionally bijective.
The diagonal action and canonical H-linear associator apply to all modules. Batch 8 uses the monoidal structure without importing finite-dimensional duality or assuming an existing braiding.

The double-module theorem uses the stated naturality, invertibility and two hexagons. The canonical-R theorem preserves c=τR and both leg-product orders, including α⁻¹ in the second hexagon. The C2 example's separate double-name mismatch is recorded in concerns.

This is contextual prerequisite material: the ordered-basis Hecke operator has independent quadratic and three-factor braid checks. The tensor-action theorem extends these locally and checks distant commutation; it does not infer a quadratic relation from a universal R-matrix.
